Wax
WAKS
v.
Old English weaxan, “to grow, increase.” Distinct from the noun wax (the substance). The KJV preserves the archaic verb in many places where modern translations use grew or became.

📖 Biblical Definition

Wax as a verb in the KJV means to grow, increase, become—an Old English word that has all but disappeared from modern English usage except in a few residual phrases (wax and wane, wax eloquent). The KJV preserves it across many passages, both of literal growth and of moral or spiritual increase. Of the boy John the Baptist: and the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit (Luke 1:80). Of the child Jesus: and the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, filled with wisdom: and the grace of God was upon him (Luke 2:40). Of the apostles after the first persecution: they spake the word of God with boldness... and the word of God increased; and the number of the disciples multiplied... and many of the priests were obedient to the faith (Acts 4:31, 6:7—the underlying verb is the same). Of the gospel’s spread under persecution: but the word of God grew and multiplied (Acts 12:24). The verb is therefore positive in many of its biblical uses. But it has a negative register also. The love of many shall wax cold, Christ says of the latter-day apostasy (Matt 24:12)—the verb naming the inverse increase, the growing-cold of love that should have been growing warm. Wax old as doth a garment, Hebrews 1:11 says of the heavens and earth which shall pass away—the increase that is the aging toward dissolution. Wax worse and worse, Paul says of evil men and seducers in the last days (2 Tim 3:13). The KJV’s retention of the verb has therefore a structural usefulness: it captures the picture of growing, increasing, becoming-more, in a single Old English word that can be applied to physical maturation, spiritual growth, moral increase (in either direction), and cosmic dissolution. Modern translations have to choose between grew, became, increased, got, depending on context; the KJV says waxed, and the reader who knows the verb knows what it covers.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines WAX as to increase in size; to grow; to become larger; to pass from one state to another; in scripture, to grow physically, spiritually, or morally in either direction.

expand to see more

WAX, v.i. — 1. To increase in size; to grow; to become larger; as the waxing and waning of the moon. 2. To pass from one state to another; to become; as, the days wax cold. The love of many shall wax cold (Matt 24:12).

WAXING, ppr. — Increasing in size or extent; growing; becoming.

📖 Key Scripture

Luke 1:80 — "And the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, and was in the deserts till the day of his shewing unto Israel."

Luke 2:40 — "And the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, filled with wisdom: and the grace of God was upon him."

Matthew 24:12 — "And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold."

Hebrews 1:11-12 — "They shall perish; but thou remainest; and they all shall wax old as doth a garment; And as a vesture shalt thou fold them up, and they shall be changed: but thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Wax as a verb has been functionally lost in modern English, replaced with several scattered alternatives (grew, became, increased); the loss is a small specimen of the general thinning of English vocabulary, and the KJV reader who recovers the verb recovers also a register of growth-and-becoming that the substitutes cannot quite reproduce.

expand to see more

Wax as a verb has been functionally lost from modern English usage, surviving only in a few residual phrases (wax eloquent, wax and wane) that retain the word as a stylized fossil rather than as a living verb. Modern translations therefore have no single equivalent and must scatter the KJV’s consistent wax across several different words (grew, became, increased, got) depending on context. The trade has its accessibility gains and its rhetorical losses. The KJV’s consistent verb captures the underlying picture of growing-becoming, applicable to the boy John, the boy Jesus, the spreading gospel, the cooling love, the aging heavens, and the worsening of evil men, in a single Anglo-Saxon word that the modernizations cannot quite consolidate. The reader who has learned the KJV verb can hold all these uses together in his mind under one word; the reader of the modernizations cannot.

This is, as with holpen and peradventure, a small specimen of the general thinning of English vocabulary that the modernization of the Bible has both registered and accelerated. The older English had more words for shades of meaning the modern English has flattened. Wax meant something the substitutes do not quite capture: not just grow, not just become, not just increase, but the specific Anglo-Saxon verb for growing-becoming that runs from the cradle through the cooling and on to the dissolution of the heavens. Recover the word in the KJV, and one recovers also access to a register modern English has narrowed. The case is not for the rejection of modern translations but for the recognition that the older vocabulary is doing work the substitutes cannot always perform, and the saint who knows both is the better-served reader of both.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English weaxan (to grow, increase); used in the KJV to render several Greek and Hebrew growth-verbs: auxanō (to grow), palaioō (to grow old), psuchō (to grow cold)—a single Anglo-Saxon word covering the picture of growing-becoming.

expand to see more

Old English weaxan — to grow, increase (the etymological root).

Greek auxanō (G837) — to grow, increase (Luke 1:80; 2:40; Acts 6:7; 12:24; 19:20).

Greek palaioō (G3822) — to make old, declare old (Heb 1:11; 8:13).

Greek psuchō (G5594) — to grow cool, cold (Matt 24:12).

Usage

"The child grew, and waxed strong in spirit—the same verb for John (Luke 1:80) and Jesus (Luke 2:40), capturing physical-and-spiritual maturation in a single word."

"The love of many shall wax cold—the negative use: the growing-becoming that runs in the direction of dissolution."

"Modern translations scatter wax across grew, became, increased; the KJV’s single Anglo-Saxon verb captures the underlying picture the substitutes thin out."
